newsitem.title: UK: UK bank takeover talk mostly froth - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK bank takeover talk mostly froth - analysts.

text.p: Rumours persist in the London stock market of possible further consolidation of Britain's banking sector.
But analysts on Wednesday said the talk could be a symptom of a stock market which is starting to need big stories to help it reach new highs.

The name in the frame in the past few days has been the giant HSBC Holdings which has been linked with Royal Bank of Scotland and Abbey National as possible partners for its UK retail and commercial bank Midland.
"If HSBC did something like that it would be a material departure from the management strategy they've been pursuing," said Tim Sykes, banking analyst at BZW.
HSBC, which has extensive international banking assets including HongkongBank, Marine Midland in the U.S. and a controlling interest in Hang Seng Bank, declined to comment on the market rumours.
The banking group has a lot of capital and has said that it will not just return this to shareholders in the form, for example, of a share buyback or inflated dividends.

In its annual results statement, HSBC reported its tier one capital ratio at a high 9.9 percent, although analysts accept that it needs high capital to back its business expansion in areas such as Asia and Latin America.
Sources close to the bank say it is very unlikely to make a major buy in the next few months especially in Britain, although it is impossible to rule out a purchase.

They say its expansion plans in Asia, where it is looking to increase its insurance market presence and in Latin America, where it recently made a major purchase in Brazil, are at the top of the agenda at the moment.

Indeed, in an interview with Reuters in March, HSBC chief executive John Bond predicted organic growth for Midland Bank as he would find the the price of acquisitions in the UK market impossible to justify to shareholders.
Analysts say that in general, large banking mergers tend not to happen at the top of the cycle, with predators more likely to move in when banking shares look cheaper than they do now.

Market strategists say that both the banking sector and the wider market are probably near the top although in recent days some have been raising their forecasts for London's FTSE 100 index this year to around 5000 compared to its current level of around 4700.
Analysts say Midland Bank has become more profitable and some question that merging it with another UK bank at this stage would be the most productive strategy.
But David Poutney, banking analyst at Panmure Gordon, said that one of the best ways of making Midland more profitable would be to merge it and take the large cost savings that would be forthcoming.
Poutney dismissed thoughts of a merger with Abbey National but saw Royal Bank, which many see as the British bank most exposed to a downturn in profitability in the sector, as a possible buy.
Such a merger would bring together First Direct, the Midland's pioneering direct banking operation, with Direct Line, Royal Bank's direct-selling channel for insurance and other financial products.
A major problem for any takeover of Royal Bank would be the political angle. A takeover of one of Scotland's major banks by a London-based international bank would not go down well in Edinburgh.
In 1996, Midland made a pre-tax profit of 1.27 billion pounds ($2.1 billion), 27 percent higher than the year before, out of pre-tax profits for the whole HSBC group of 4.52 billion pounds.

Other takeover targets in the banking sector are likely to be the building societies which are converting to bank status and coming to the market this year, with the exception of mortgage market leader Halifax which is seen as too big for anyone to swallow.

Alliance & Leicester which was floated to market last month, was trading today at over six pounds per share, a price which analysts say a substantial bid premium and may overvalue in terms of fundamentals.

"We've had a big merger this week (GrandMet and Guinness) and the market is looking for more news to make it move," said one analyst. "That could have as much to do with these rumours as any logic to do with the bank sector."
($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
